_meta.description: Reviewed enrichment (enrich.py schema: pronunciation, semanticRange, related, notes) for entries whose headline fix_dominant_senses.py corrected but whose enriched prose still described the displaced sense, homonym or proper name (e.g. 'wilderness' described a mouth, 'horse' a swallow). Written to enrich.py's rules and grounded on STEP TBESH definitions and TAHOT renderings. Applied by scripts/apply_enrichment.py.

semanticRange: dejectedly, in a subdued way (of walking)

related.note: prepositional form; 'gently, slowly' in most occurrences
adjective 'tender, soft'; overlapping sense of gentleness

H0328.notes: The word denotes a gentle, unhurried manner. David's charge to 'deal gently' with Absalom (2 Sam 18:5) uses it, and Isaiah 8:6 contrasts the 'gently flowing' waters of Shiloah, a picture of God's quiet provision, with the flood of Assyria.

semanticRange: leader of a tribal division or clan

related.note: thousand, clan unit; possible etymological link
prince, tribal leader; comparable title
LXX rendering, leader or governor

H0441.notes: Used as a title for the clan chiefs descended from Esau, listed in a long roll in Gen 36:15-43. Zechariah later applies it to the leaders of Judah (Zech 12:5-6).

semanticRange: clothes torn in grief or alarm

related.note: outer garment, mantle; near synonym
clothing, apparel; general synonym
usual LXX equivalent for garment

H0899.notes: The everyday word for clothing, used for any garment without distinction. It carries much of the narrative weight in the Joseph story: Reuben tears his garments over the empty pit (Gen 37:29), and Joseph flees leaving his garment in the hand of Potiphar's wife (Gen 39:12).

semanticRange: to lay waste, devastate a land

related.note: emptiness, desolation (Nah 2:10)
jar; wordplay in Jer 19:1, 7
to be desolate; parallel term

H1238.notes: Isaiah's apocalypse opens with the LORD emptying the earth and laying it waste, "utterly emptied and utterly plundered" (Isa 24:1, 3). Jeremiah plays on the sound of a clay jar (baqbuq) when God declares he will make void the plans of Judah (Jer 19:7).

related.note: the ordinary Hebrew verb 'to be'; havah is its rarer by-form
Aramaic equivalent 'to be', frequent in Daniel and Ezra
the divine name, often linked by scholars to this 'to be' root

H1933.notes: A rarer, largely poetic by-form of הָיָה 'to be', used for existing or coming to pass (Gen 27:29; Eccl 2:22). It matters chiefly because the divine name is often connected to this 'to be' root in discussions of Exodus 3:14.

semanticRange: to warn of danger or judgment
to teach, admonish in God's statutes

related.note: Aramaic equivalent; to take heed
watchman; the role tied to warning in Ezekiel
Hiphil: to warn solemnly, testify against

H2094.notes: Ezekiel is made a watchman who must warn the wicked; if he fails, their blood is on his hands (Ezek 3:17-21). Jethro advises Moses to teach the people the statutes and laws (Exod 18:20), and the psalmist says God's ordinances warn his servant (Ps 19:11).

semanticRange: to profane, desecrate what is holy
to put to common use, e.g. a vineyard

related.note: common, profane; the opposite of holy
to sanctify; antonym of profaning
to be unclean; overlapping cultic term

H2490.notes: In priestly and prophetic texts it denotes treating the holy as common: Israel is warned not to profane the name of God (Lev 19:12), and Ezekiel makes the profaning of that name among the nations a central charge (Ezek 36:20-23). The Hiphil carries the separate, frequent sense "to begin," as in Gen 4:26.

semanticRange: to receive a prophetic or revelatory dream
to dream falsely, of false prophets

related.note: dream; the noun from the same root
vision; parallel revelatory term
LXX equivalent, to dream

H2492.notes: Joseph's dreams set the family drama in motion (Gen 37:5-10), and dreams carry God's message to Pharaoh's officials (Gen 40:5-8). The verb is also used of prophetic dreaming, positively in Joel 2:28 (MT 3:1) and with suspicion toward the "dreamer of dreams" in Deut 13:1-5.

semanticRange: son of Gilead by a prostitute
maker of a rash vow concerning his daughter

related.note: Gilead; his father and home region
judge; the role he held for six years
NT form; listed among the faithful in Hebrews

H3316.notes: Driven out by his half-brothers, Jephthah was recalled by Gilead's elders to fight Ammon (Judg 11:1-11). His vow to offer whatever first came out of his house ended in grief when his daughter met him (Judg 11:30-40), yet Hebrews 11:32 still names him among the faithful.

related.note: might, mighty deeds; close synonym
strength, power; frequent poetic parallel
vigor, generative strength

H3581.notes: A broad word for capacity to act, used of people, animals and God alike. Jacob calls Reuben "my might" (Gen 49:3), and the soil withholds its strength, its yield, from Cain (Gen 4:12). Its best-known use is the contrast in Zech 4:6: "not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit."

semanticRange: talent, a large weight of metal
sum of money reckoned in talents

related.note: Aramaic equivalent; talent
shekel; about 3,000 made one talent
LXX equivalent; talent weight

H3603.notes: As a weight it denotes the talent, roughly 3,000 shekels; the tabernacle lampstand and its utensils required a talent of pure gold (Exod 25:39). Etymologically the word is tied to roundness, which explains its other uses: the round plain of the Jordan that Lot chose (Gen 13:10-11) and a round loaf of bread.

related.note: the common word for a full-grown ram
young lamb; frequent in sacrificial lists

H3733.notes: The word denotes a young ram or lamb, counted as wealth and tribute (Mesha of Moab paid Israel 100,000 lambs, 2 Kgs 3:4). In Ezekiel's siege oracles (Ezek 4:2; 21:22) the same word names a battering-ram, likely from the butting ram.

semanticRange: to dig a well or cistern
to dig a pit, often as a trap

related.note: to dig, search out; close synonym
pit or cistern, the thing dug
pit, often a trap or the grave

H3738.notes: Isaac's servants dig a well (Gen 26:25), and Exodus legislates for someone who digs a pit and leaves it uncovered (Exod 21:33). The Psalms turn the image into a moral pattern: the wicked man digs a pit and falls into it himself (Ps 7:15). In Ps 40:6 God has "dug" ears for the psalmist, opening them to hear.

semanticRange: jaw or jawbone of an animal
struck cheek as a sign of insult
jaws restrained, as with a bridle

related.note: tooth; often paired with jaw imagery
jaws, palate; a near synonym in poetry
LXX equivalent; jaw or cheek

H3895.notes: The word lights up in Samson's fresh jawbone of a donkey, with which he struck down a thousand men (Judg 15:15-16), the episode that gave the site its name. On a person it denotes the cheek, and a blow to the cheek is a public insult, as when Zedekiah strikes Micaiah (1 Kgs 22:24).

related.note: steppe, desert plain; frequent parallel
wasteland, desolate region
standard LXX and NT equivalent

H4057.notes: Not necessarily sandy desert but land beyond settled farming, often used for grazing: Moses leads Jethro's flock to the far side of the wilderness (Exod 3:1). It is also where Israel wanders and is tested, and in prophecy where a way for the LORD is prepared (Isa 40:3). One etymology links it to driving flocks, though that is uncertain.

semanticRange: step or stair of a staircase
ascent, as in the Psalm titles' Songs of Ascents
(rare) what comes up into the mind

related.note: to go up; the verbal root behind the noun
ascent, slope, as of a hill or pass
LXX equivalent; step, ascent

H4609.notes: Most often it refers to physical steps, from the altar that must have none (Exod 20:26) to the shadow moving back on Ahaz's steps as a sign to Hezekiah (2 Kgs 20:9-11). Its best-known use is the title of Psalms 120-134, the Songs of Ascents, usually linked to pilgrims going up to Jerusalem.

semanticRange: net or snare used in hunting
figurative trap of God or of a person

related.note: to hunt; the root behind the noun (etymology)
net; the common term for a trapping net
stronghold; related form from the same root

H4685.notes: Job feels hunted when he complains that God has closed his net around him (Job 19:6), and Ecclesiastes compares people caught by sudden misfortune to fish taken in a cruel net (Eccl 9:12). In Eccl 9:14 the same word refers to great siegeworks built against a small city.

semanticRange: God as a fortress for the faithful

related.note: crag, rock; paired with fortress in David's song
high refuge; a near synonym in the Psalms
Zion; the stronghold David captured

H4686.notes: It denotes the strongholds David held while fleeing Saul (1 Sam 22:4-5) and the stronghold of Zion he captured, which became the City of David (2 Sam 5:7). David then turns the image toward God: "The LORD is my rock and my fortress" (2 Sam 22:2; Ps 18:2).

semanticRange: rebellious, describing a people or house

related.note: to rebel, be defiant; the related verb
to revolt; a near synonym for rebellion
transgression; covenant rebellion in another key

H4805.notes: Samuel tells Saul that rebellion is as the sin of divination (1 Sam 15:23), placing defiance alongside idolatry. Ezekiel repeatedly calls Israel a "rebellious house" (Ezek 2:5), using the word in construct as a description of the people's settled character.

semanticRange: to go around, encircle a place
to surround, close in on someone
to complete a circuit, as of festivals
to round off, as hair at the temples

related.note: to turn, go around; the common synonym
circuit, turning of the year; related noun
LXX equivalent; to encircle

H5362.notes: Israel is told to go around Jericho once a day for six days (Josh 6:3), and Aram's army surrounds Elisha at Dothan (2 Kgs 6:14). Leviticus uses it for rounding off the hair at the sides of the head (Lev 19:27).

semanticRange: horse, esp. war or chariot horse
symbol of military power and self-reliance

related.note: chariotry; constantly paired with horses
horseman, cavalry steed
LXX and NT equivalent, horse

H5483.notes: In Israel's world the horse is mainly a weapon of war, so it often stands for military strength. Miriam's song celebrates the horse and its rider thrown into the sea (Exod 15:1, 21), and Ps 20:7 contrasts trust in chariots and horses with trust in the name of the LORD.

semanticRange: to be overwhelmed, of the spirit

related.note: faint, weary; related adjective of exhaustion
weary, tired; near synonym
to stumble, totter from weakness

H5848.notes: Describes physical or inner fainting. Jacob leaves the feeble animals of the flock to Laban (Gen 30:42), while the psalmist cries out "when my heart is faint" (Ps 61:2) and Jonah remembers the LORD "when my soul fainted within me" (Jonah 2:7).

semanticRange: Mount Ebal, mountain of the curse near Shechem
Ebal, a Horite descendant of Seir
Ebal, son of Joktan (also called Obal)

related.note: facing mountain of blessing across the valley
spelling of Joktan's son in Gen 10:28
city in the valley between the two mountains

H5858.notes: Mostly a place name: Moses commands that the curses be pronounced from Ebal, opposite Gerizim (Deut 11:29; 27:13), and Joshua builds an altar there (Josh 8:30). The same spelling also names a Horite (Gen 36:23) and a son of Joktan (1 Chr 1:22); the etymology ("bare" or "stone") is uncertain.

semanticRange: to sing responsively, raise one's voice

related.note: noun 'answer, reply' from the same root
Aramaic equivalent 'to answer', common in Daniel
usual LXX rendering, 'to answer'

H6030.notes: The word denotes responding to what has been said or done, from a simple reply to legal testimony (Exod 20:16, 'you shall not bear false witness'). The Psalms' repeated cry 'answer me, O LORD' (Ps 4:1; 27:7) asks God to respond to prayer with action, not only words.

semanticRange: to humble, humiliate, including sexual violation
to humble oneself, as in fasting

related.note: poor, afflicted; the person who suffers this
affliction, misery; the related noun
humble, meek; the positive side of lowliness

H6031.notes: Abram is told his descendants will be afflicted four hundred years (Gen 15:13), fulfilled when Egypt set taskmasters to afflict Israel (Exod 1:11-12). On the Day of Atonement Israel was to "afflict your souls," usually understood as fasting (Lev 16:29), and the psalmist can say it was good for him to be afflicted (Ps 119:71).

semanticRange: to be simple, naive, easily misled

related.note: simple, naive person, easily led
to deceive (Hiphil); near synonym
LXX equivalent, to deceive

H6601.notes: Covers luring someone by persuasion or deceit: the law addresses a man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin (Exod 22:16), and the Philistines urge Delilah to entice Samson (Judg 16:5). Jeremiah uses it daringly of God: "You deceived me, O LORD, and I was deceived" (Jer 20:7).

semanticRange: large body shield covering the whole frame
God's faithfulness as a protective shield

related.note: smaller round shield; often paired with this word
buckler; paired with it in Ps 91:4
LXX equivalent; large door-shaped shield

H6793.notes: A shield-bearer carried Goliath's large shield before him (1 Sam 17:7, 41), and Solomon made two hundred such shields of beaten gold (1 Kgs 10:16). Poetically, God's faithfulness is a body shield and buckler around the one who trusts him (Ps 91:4).

related.note: enemy; the most frequent parallel term
to show hostility; verb behind the noun
adversary, opponent; near synonym

H6862.notes: Denotes the hostile party, personal or national: Melchizedek blesses God who delivered Abram's enemies into his hand (Gen 14:20). The Song of Moses has God taking vengeance on his adversaries (Deut 32:41, 43). A separate homograph denoting "distress" or "narrowness" shares the spelling (Deut 4:30).

semanticRange: to show hostility, be an adversary
to make a rival, as of a second wife

related.note: adversary, foe; the related noun
enemy; frequently paired with this word
rival wife; also distress

H6887.notes: God promises Israel, "I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries" (Exod 23:22). Moses is told to harass the Midianites because they had vexed Israel at Peor (Num 25:17-18). The participle often stands simply for the people's foes.

semanticRange: pity shown by one person to another

related.note: 'womb'; the same root, often linked to motherly tenderness
verb 'to have compassion, show mercy'
covenant loyalty; frequently paired with rachamim

H7356.notes: A plural of intensity naming deep, tender compassion, used above all of God (Lam 3:22, 'his mercies never come to an end'). Its link to רֶחֶם 'womb' is a real shared root, but context, not etymology, carries the sense of mercy in each passage.

semanticRange: to shepherd, tend, pasture a flock
to rule or care for a people (of leaders, of God)

related.note: participle used as noun 'shepherd'
'pasture, feeding place' from the same root
LXX and NT equivalent 'to shepherd' (John 21:16)

H7462.notes: The word denotes tending and feeding a flock, and becomes a central image for leadership. 'The LORD is my shepherd' (Ps 23:1) uses its participle, and Ezekiel 34 indicts Israel's leaders as shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock, before God promises to shepherd them himself.

semanticRange: ear, head of grain on the stalk

related.note: standing grain in the field
ear of grain plucked by hand
LXX and NT equivalent, ear of grain

H7641.notes: Pharaoh's second dream turns on seven full ears of grain swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones (Gen 41:5-7), and Ruth asks to glean ears of grain (Ruth 2:2). The famous password test at the Jordan (Judg 12:6) uses this spelling, though whether it refers to an ear of grain or a stream is debated.

related.note: three; possible origin of the title (etymology)
commander, official; a broader term for rank
LXX equivalent; officer, literally third-man

H7991.notes: Pharaoh's chariots go out with officers over all of them (Exod 14:7). The title may once have named the third man in a chariot, though that is etymology, not its sense in use. Its most vivid appearance is the royal officer on whose arm the king leaned, who doubted Elisha's word and was trampled in the gate (2 Kgs 7:2, 17).

semanticRange: male goat, buck, esp. for sin offering

related.note: goat (female or generic)
he-goat, ram; synonym, also of leaders
destination of the scapegoat (Lev 16)

H8163.notes: The standard sacrificial male goat of Leviticus, prescribed for a ruler's sin offering (Lev 4:23-24) and at the heart of the Day of Atonement ritual (Lev 16). The word is related to the adjective "hairy," used of Esau (Gen 27:11), and in Lev 17:7 it refers to goat idols or demons.

semanticRange: royal scribe of King Josiah of Judah
reader of the rediscovered Book of the Law
father of Ahikam, Gemariah, and Elasah

related.note: Hilkiah; high priest who handed Shaphan the book
Ahikam; son who protected Jeremiah
Gedaliah; grandson, governor after Jerusalem fell

H8227.notes: Shaphan was the secretary to whom Hilkiah gave the Book of the Law found in the temple, and he read it before Josiah, sparking the king's reform (2 Kgs 22:8-10). His family stayed loyal to Jeremiah: his son Ahikam protected the prophet (Jer 26:24). The name is the same word as the rock hyrax, an etymological link only.

semanticRange: armor as a figure of protection

related.note: helmet; listed with armor in battle equipment
Greek 'breastplate', the LXX-era equivalent

H8302.notes: The word denotes a soldier's coat of mail, such as Goliath's bronze scale armor (1 Sam 17:5) and the armor Saul gave David (1 Sam 17:38). Isaiah 59:17 pictures God putting on righteousness 'as a breastplate', an image Paul echoes in Ephesians 6:14.

semanticRange: tabernacle curtains and veil of twisted linen
priestly and royal garments of fine linen
costly cloth as a mark of wealth

related.note: later Hebrew term for fine linen, byssus
flax, the plant linen is spun from
LXX equivalent for fine linen

H8336.notes: Egypt's prized white linen: Pharaoh clothes Joseph in garments of shesh when he elevates him (Gen 41:42). In Exodus it is the signature fabric of the tabernacle, its curtains made of "fine twisted linen" with blue, purple and scarlet (Exod 26:1).

semanticRange: ground of hope, what one trusts in

related.note: to wait for, look eagerly toward
expectation; a near synonym in Proverbs
LXX equivalent; hope

H8615.notes: Job wrestles with the word, asking where his hope is when his days run out (Job 7:6). Through Jeremiah, God promises the exiles "a future and a hope" (Jer 29:11), and Hosea pictures the Valley of Achor becoming a door of hope (Hos 2:15). The same form names Rahab's scarlet cord (Josh 2:18).
